warmup.q: A Vert.x HTTP handler wraps its 500 ms JDBC call in vertx.executeBlocking(() -> dao.query()). Four requests arrive at the same moment on a server with one event loop. Roughly how long until all four are answered?
options: About 500 ms: the four queries run in parallel on the worker pool
About 2,000 ms: by default executeBlocking runs calls from the same context one after another
About 500 ms, but only if the worker pool has at least 4 threads
It never finishes: executeBlocking deadlocks on a single event loop
warmup.why: executeBlocking is ordered by default, and all requests to one HTTP server share its context. The loop is free, but the four queries queue behind each other on the worker pool. This lesson's demo measured 2,012 ms ordered and 511 ms with executeBlocking(callable, false). The default worker pool has 20 threads, so the pool size isn't the limit.

sections.h: Vert.x puts a context on top of Netty's event loop
sections.html:
Vert.x 5.2.3 runs on Netty 4.2.20. A Vertx instance starts a group of Netty event loops, twice the number of cores by default (8 on a 4-core machine), named vert.x-eventloop-thread-0 and up. Its HTTP server is a Netty pipeline like the one in lesson 3, and the stack trace later in this lesson ends in io.netty.channel.SingleThreadIoEventLoop.run, the same loop class.

What Vert.x adds is a set of rules over those loops. The central one is the context: the home of a piece of code, which decides the thread that runs it. Most contexts are event-loop contexts, each tied to one event loop for life. When you register a handler, Vert.x remembers the current context, and every call of that handler runs there. The Vert.x docs promise that a handler is never executed concurrently and, worker verticles aside, always runs on the same event loop thread. That is lesson 3's Netty rule, one channel, one loop, extended to all your code: HTTP handlers, timers and event-bus consumers.

The second change is the API. Vert.x 4 had two styles, callbacks and futures. Vert.x 5 kept only futures: every asynchronous method returns an io.vertx.core.Future, and the callback overloads are gone.

Java
// Vert.x 5: listen returns a Future
server.listen(8080).onSuccess(s -> System.out.println("listening on " + s.actualPort()));
// Vert.x 4 style no longer compiles:
// server.listen(8080, ar -> ...)  ->  error: incompatible types: String is not a functional interface
Kotlin
// Vert.x 5: listen returns a Future
server.listen(8080).onSuccess { s -> println("listening on ${s.actualPort()}") }
// Vert.x 4 style no longer compiles:
// server.listen(8080) { ar -> ... }   the only two-argument listen left is listen(int, String)

The Java error looks unrelated because the compiler matched the one remaining two-argument overload, listen(int, String), and complains that a String isn't a lambda. The same migration replaced executeBlocking(promise -> ...) with a version that takes a Callable and returns a Future.

try.title: Hit the Vert.x 5 API change
steps: In ContextsDemo.java, add one line after Vertx vertx = Vertx.vertx();: vertx.createHttpServer().listen(8080, ar -> {});.
Predict whether it compiles. Then run the demo with the command below.
try.expect: Compilation fails with error: incompatible types: String is not a functional interface. The callback overload of listen no longer exists in Vert.x 5, so javac tries listen(int, String) and can't turn your lambda into a String.

sections.h: Verticles: units you deploy, each with its own context
sections.html:
A verticle is a class you deploy into Vert.x, and deploying it gives each instance its own context. In Vert.x 5 you extend VerticleBase and return a Future from start(), so the deployment completes only when your setup has:

Java
public class AuthorizeVerticle extends VerticleBase {
    @Override
    public Future<?> start() {
        return vertx.eventBus().<JsonObject>consumer("payments.authorize", msg ->
                msg.reply(new JsonObject().put("status", "APPROVED"))
        ).completion();                                  // done when the consumer is registered
    }
}

vertx.deployVerticle(AuthorizeVerticle::new, new DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2));
Kotlin
class AuthorizeVerticle : VerticleBase() {
    override fun start(): Future<*> =
        vertx.eventBus().consumer<JsonObject>("payments.authorize") { msg ->
            msg.reply(JsonObject().put("status", "APPROVED"))
        }.completion()                                   // done when the consumer is registered
}

vertx.deployVerticle(::AuthorizeVerticle, DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2))

For two instances you pass a factory, because each instance must be its own object. In 5.2.3 that factory is a Supplier, though the docs still say Callable. Each instance gets its own event-loop context, usually on different loops, which is how one verticle class uses several cores. Inside one instance, code never runs on two threads at once, so its fields need no locks.

The threading model in DeploymentOptions decides what kind of context a verticle gets. This section's demo prints where each kind runs:

[EVENT_LOOP] start() on vert.x-eventloop-thread-0 eventLoopCtx=true workerCtx=false
[WORKER] start() on vert.x-worker-thread-0 eventLoopCtx=false workerCtx=true
[VIRTUAL_THREAD] start() on vert.x-virtual-thread-0 (virtual) eventLoopCtx=false workerCtx=false

EVENT_LOOP, the default, must never block. A WORKER verticle runs on the worker pool (20 threads by default) and may block; it still never runs on two threads at once, though successive calls can land on different worker threads. VIRTUAL_THREAD is new in Vert.x 5 and needs Java 21: the verticle runs on virtual threads, and future.await() parks the virtual thread until the result arrives. It also runs one task at a time, with one catch from the docs: a field you read before an await() may have changed after it, because another task of the same verticle can run while you wait.

try.title: Where does each verticle run?
steps: Open ContextsDemo.java (or ContextsDemo.kt). It deploys one verticle per threading model, then calls executeBlocking from an event-loop context.
Predict the thread name in each line, and on which thread onSuccess runs after executeBlocking.

code.title: ContextsDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.nio.l05; import io.vertx.core.Context; import io.vertx.core.DeploymentOptions; import io.vertx.core.Future; import io.vertx.core.ThreadingModel; import io.vertx.core.VerticleBase; import io.vertx.core.Vertx; import io.vertx.core.VertxOptions; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** Where does a verticle's code run? One verticle per threading model, plus executeBlocking. */ public class ContextsDemo { static String where() { Thread t = Thread.currentThread(); Context c = Vertx.currentContext(); return t.getName() + (t.isVirtual() ? " (virtual)" : "") + " eventLoopCtx=" + c.isEventLoopContext() + " workerCtx=" + c.isWorkerContext(); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println("default event loops: " + VertxOptions.DEFAULT_EVENT_LOOP_POOL_SIZE + " (cpus=" + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() + "), default worker pool: " + VertxOptions.DEFAULT_WORKER_POOL_SIZE); Vertx vertx = Vertx.vertx(); for (ThreadingModel model : List.of(ThreadingModel.EVENT_LOOP, ThreadingModel.WORKER, ThreadingModel.VIRTUAL_THREAD)) { await(vertx.deployVerticle(new VerticleBase() { @Override public Future<?> start() { System.out.println("[" + model + "] start() on " + where()); return Future.succeededFuture(); } }, new DeploymentOptions().setThreadingModel(model))); } vertx.runOnContext(v -> vertx.executeBlocking(() -> Thread.currentThread().getName()) .onSuccess(name -> System.out.println("[executeBlocking] callable ran on " + name + ", onSuccess runs on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()))); Thread.sleep(300); await(vertx.close()); } static <T> T await(Future<T> f) throws Exception { return f.toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } }

try.expect: The first line reports 8 event loops on 4 CPUs and a worker pool of 20. The three verticles start on vert.x-eventloop-thread-0, vert.x-worker-thread-0 and a virtual thread vert.x-virtual-thread-0. The executeBlocking callable runs on a worker thread, and onSuccess runs back on an event-loop thread: the context that called it.

sections.h: The event bus carries messages between contexts
sections.html:
The event bus is how verticles talk without sharing objects. There is one per Vertx instance, and an address is just a string such as payments.authorize. You can send in three ways:

  • send(address, msg): to one consumer at that address, chosen round-robin.
  • request(address, msg): to one consumer, and you get a Future of its reply.
  • publish(address, msg): to every consumer at that address.

This section's demo deploys two instances of a greeter and makes requests:

request greet #0 -> hello dev0 from instance#1 on vert.x-eventloop-thread-1
request greet #1 -> hello dev1 from instance#2 on vert.x-eventloop-thread-0
request greet #2 -> hello dev2 from instance#1 on vert.x-eventloop-thread-1
request nobody -> NO_HANDLERS code=-1 message=No handlers for address nobody
request fail -> RECIPIENT_FAILURE code=42 message=boom from instance#2
request silent (timeout 300 ms) -> TIMEOUT after 311 ms

A request can fail in three ways, each delivered as a ReplyException with a failureType(). NO_HANDLERS means nobody listens at the address. RECIPIENT_FAILURE means the consumer called msg.fail(code, text), and you get its code and text. TIMEOUT means no reply arrived in time. The default timeout is 30 seconds, far too long for a payment path, so set one per request with new DeliveryOptions().setSendTimeout(...).

The reply comes back on the requester's context, not the consumer's. A worker verticle that sends a request handles the reply on a worker thread; a virtual-thread verticle resumes on its virtual thread.

Two properties keep the event bus from being a message broker. Delivery is best effort: there is no persistence and no retry, and the docs tell you to make handlers idempotent. And inside one JVM a message can be handed over by reference. With a custom local codec whose transform returns its argument, the consumer receives the very object you sent, so never change a message after you send it. Built-in codecs cover strings, numbers, Buffer, JsonObject and JsonArray; other types need a codec you register.

try.title: Make every kind of reply happen
steps: Open EventBusDemo.java (or EventBusDemo.kt). Predict which instance answers each of the four requests, and how many lines publish prints.

import io.vertx.core.eventbus.EventBus; import io.vertx.core.eventbus.ReplyException; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** Point-to-point, publish/subscribe and the three ways a request can fail. */ public class EventBusDemo { static final AtomicInteger IDS = new AtomicInteger(); public static class Greeter extends VerticleBase { final int id = IDS.incrementAndGet(); @Override public Future<?> start() { EventBus eb = vertx.eventBus(); eb.<String>consumer("greet", m -> m.reply("hello " + m.body() + " from instance#" + id + " on " + Thread.currentThread().getName())); eb.<String>consumer("news", m -> System.out.println(" [news] instance#" + id + " got '" + m.body() + "'")); eb.<String>consumer("fail", m -> m.fail(42, "boom from instance#" + id)); return eb.<String>consumer("silent", m -> { /* never replies */ }).completion(); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Vertx vertx = Vertx.vertx(); EventBus eb = vertx.eventBus(); await(vertx.deployVerticle(Greeter::new, new DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2))); for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) System.out.println("request greet #" + i + " -> " + await(eb.<String>request("greet", "dev" + i)).body()); System.out.println("publish news:"); eb.publish("news", "release 1.0"); Thread.sleep(200); for (String address : List.of("nobody", "fail")) { try { await(eb.request(address, "x")); } catch (ExecutionException e) { ReplyException re = (ReplyException) e.getCause(); System.out.println("request " + address + " -> " + re.failureType() + " code=" + re.failureCode() + " message=" + re.getMessage()); } } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); try { await(eb.request("silent", "x", new DeliveryOptions().setSendTimeout(300))); } catch (ExecutionException e) { ReplyException re = (ReplyException) e.getCause(); System.out.println("request silent (timeout 300 ms) -> " + re.failureType() + " after " + (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 + " ms"); } System.out.println("default request timeout: " + DeliveryOptions.DEFAULT_TIMEOUT + " ms"); await(vertx.close()); } static <T> T await(Future<T> f) throws Exception { return f.toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } }

The failures come back as NO_HANDLERS, RECIPIENT_FAILURE with code 42, and TIMEOUT after about 300 ms. With 1,000 ms the timeout simply arrives later: the consumer still never replies.

sections.h: The golden rule, and the catch in executeBlocking
sections.html:
Vert.x calls it the golden rule: don't block the event loop. Its docs list what counts: Thread.sleep(), waiting on a lock or a synchronized monitor, a long database operation, a complex calculation, spinning in a loop. They also give the budget: with one event loop and 10,000 HTTP requests a second, each request can take at most 0.1 ms.

Vert.x checks the rule for you. A separate thread, vertx-blocked-thread-checker, wakes up every second and looks at each event loop. If the task a loop is running started more than 2 seconds ago, it logs a warning, and past 5 seconds it adds the blocked thread's stack trace. It measures one task at a time: each loop records when its current task began, and the checker compares that with the clock. So ten 300 ms blocking calls in a row hold a loop for 3 seconds and never produce a warning. This section's demo sleeps 6 seconds on an event loop:

[vertx-blocked-thread-checker] WARN io.vertx.core.impl.BlockedThreadChecker - Thread vert.x-eventloop-thread-0 has been blocked for 2891 ms, time limit is 2000 ms
[vertx-blocked-thread-checker] WARN io.vertx.core.impl.BlockedThreadChecker - Thread vert.x-eventloop-thread-0 has been blocked for 3891 ms, time limit is 2000 ms
...
io.vertx.core.VertxException: Thread blocked
	at java.base/java.lang.Thread.sleep(Thread.java:509)
	at workbench.nio.l05.BlockedThreadDemo.lambda$main$0(BlockedThreadDemo.java:13)
	...
	at io.netty.channel.SingleThreadIoEventLoop.run(SingleThreadIoEventLoop.java:228)

The first warning came at 2.9 s, not 2.0 s, because the checker only looks once a second. Search your logs for has been blocked for; the logger is io.vertx.core.impl.BlockedThreadChecker. The checker only reports. It never interrupts the blocked thread.

For blocking work there is executeBlocking: it runs a Callable on the worker pool and completes a Future back on your context. Its catch is that it is ordered by default, so calls from the same context run one after another. The demo sends 4 concurrent HTTP requests, each doing a 500 ms fake JDBC call, to a server with one event loop:

block-on-event-loop        4 requests x 500 ms -> 2201 ms, ran on [vert.x-eventloop-thread-0]
executeBlocking-ordered    4 requests x 500 ms -> 2012 ms, ran on [vert.x-worker-thread-0]
executeBlocking-unordered  4 requests x 500 ms ->  511 ms, ran on [vert.x-worker-thread-0, ..., vert.x-worker-thread-3]

The ordered version freed the event loop for every other connection, but the four queries still ran single file, because every request to one server shares that server's context. Pass false when the calls are independent: executeBlocking(callable, false). And remember what the worker pool is: 20 threads by default, a bounded pool like the ones in the executors track. Behind a 20-connection JDBC pool, that is a thread-per-request design again. That is fine, as long as you size it like one.

try.title: Three ways to make a slow call
steps: Open ExecuteBlockingDemo.java (or ExecuteBlockingDemo.kt). Predict the total time and the thread names for each of the three modes.
Run it with the command below.

Then run ./gradlew :nio:demo -Pmain=workbench.nio.l05.BlockedThreadDemo and predict when the first warning appears and when the stack trace appears. Run it with -Pargs=2500 too: how many warnings now?

code.title: ExecuteBlockingDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.nio.l05; import io.vertx.core.Vertx; import io.vertx.core.VertxOptions; import io.vertx.core.http.HttpServer; import java.net.URI; import java.net.http.HttpRequest; import java.net.http.HttpResponse; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.Set; import java.util.TreeSet; import java.util.concurrent.Callable; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** One event loop, an HTTP server, 4 concurrent requests that each make a 500 ms "JDBC call". Three ways. */ public class ExecuteBlockingDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { for (String mode : List.of("block-on-event-loop", "executeBlocking-ordered", "executeBlocking-unordered")) { Vertx vertx = Vertx.vertx(new VertxOptions().setEventLoopPoolSize(1)); Callable<String> fakeJdbc = () -> { Thread.sleep(500); return Thread.currentThread().getName(); }; HttpServer server = vertx.createHttpServer().requestHandler(req -> { switch (mode) { case "block-on-event-loop" -> { try { req.response().end(fakeJdbc.call()); // blocks the loop } catch (Exception e) { req.response().setStatusCode(500).end(); } } case "executeBlocking-ordered" -> // the default: ordered = true vertx.executeBlocking(fakeJdbc).onComplete(ar -> req.response().end(ar.result())); default -> vertx.executeBlocking(fakeJdbc, false).onComplete(ar -> req.response().end(ar.result())); } }).listen(0, "127.0.0.1").toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(); java.net.http.HttpClient client = java.net.http.HttpClient.newBuilder() .proxy(java.net.http.HttpClient.Builder.NO_PROXY).build(); URI uri = URI.create("http://127.0.0.1:" + server.actualPort() + "/"); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); List<CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>>> calls = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { calls.add(client.sendAsync(HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri).build(), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString())); } Set<String> threads = new TreeSet<>(); for (var call : calls) threads.add(call.get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS).body()); System.out.printf("%-26s 4 requests x 500 ms -> %4d ms, ran on %s%n", mode, (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, threads); vertx.close().toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(); } } }

try.expect: About 2,000 ms on the event loop thread, about 2,000 ms on one worker thread with the ordered default, and about 500 ms across four worker threads with false (2,201, 2,012 and 511 ms in my run; this track's research run measured 2,814, 2,043 and 576). The blocked-thread demo warns between 2 and 3 seconds in, once a second after that, and adds the VertxException: Thread blocked stack trace after 5 seconds. A 2,500 ms sleep gives zero or one warning, depending on when the checker happens to look.

refs.title: Vert.x 5.2.3 core documentation: The Golden Rule (source)

analogy: A Vert.x context is a desk with one chair. Everything registered at that desk (handlers, timers, event-bus consumers) is dealt with by whoever sits in the chair, one item at a time, so nobody at the desk needs to lock the drawers. An event-loop desk always has the same clerk; the event bus is the internal mail between desks; executeBlocking is sending a long errand to the back office and getting the result back on your desk. The analogy breaks for worker desks: different clerks can sit in a worker desk's chair on different days, though never two at once, which is why a worker verticle is still single-threaded but not tied to one thread.
world: Every Quarkus service you run is a Vert.x application underneath: the HTTP layer is a Vert.x server on Vert.x event loops, and Quarkus's @ConsumeEvent sits on the same event bus. The blocked-thread warning in this lesson is the one you will see in a Quarkus log when an endpoint blocks an IO thread, with Quarkus-specific limits that lesson 6 covers. If a team writes plain Vert.x for a payment router or a ledger projection, make them pass false to executeBlocking for independent queries, set a send timeout on every event-bus request, and keep handlers idempotent, because the event bus will not redeliver a lost message.
mistake: The common mistake is moving blocking code into executeBlocking and calling the job done. The event loop is free, so the warnings stop, but the default is ordered per context, and every request to one HTTP server or one consumer shares a context, so the calls still queue behind each other: 2,012 ms instead of 511 ms in this lesson's demo. Pass false for independent calls, or deploy a WORKER verticle with several instances. The second mistake is waiting for a result on the event loop, with toCompletionStage().toCompletableFuture().get(): if the result needs that same loop to complete, the thread waits for itself.

compare.title: A verticle that offloads a blocking query

java.title: BalanceVerticle.java
java.html: public class BalanceVerticle extends VerticleBase { @Override public Future<?> start() { return vertx.eventBus().<String>consumer("ledger.balance", msg -> vertx.executeBlocking(() -> LedgerDao.balanceCents(msg.body()), false) .onSuccess(msg::reply) // back on this verticle's context .onFailure(e -> msg.fail(500, e.getMessage())) ).completion(); } } vertx.deployVerticle(BalanceVerticle::new, new DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2));

kotlin.title: BalanceVerticle.kt
kotlin.html: class BalanceVerticle : VerticleBase() { override fun start(): Future<*> = vertx.eventBus().consumer<String>("ledger.balance") { msg -> val query = Callable<Long> { LedgerDao.balanceCents(msg.body()) } vertx.executeBlocking(query, false) .onSuccess { cents: Long -> msg.reply(cents) } // back on this verticle's context .onFailure { e -> msg.fail(500, e.message) } }.completion() } vertx.deployVerticle(::BalanceVerticle, DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2))

compare.note: Same Vert.x API, same threads at runtime. Two Kotlin wrinkles came up while building this lesson's demos. vertx.deployVerticle({ BalanceVerticle() }, options) does not compile in Kotlin: Deployable is itself a single-method interface, so a bare lambda matches both overloads. Use a constructor reference (::BalanceVerticle) or Supplier { BalanceVerticle() }. And some Vert.x 5 signatures carry a @Nullable type annotation from vertx-codegen, which is not on the classpath, so Kotlin can fail with "Type annotation class 'io.vertx.codegen.annotations.Nullable' of the inferred type is inaccessible" when it infers a lambda's type. Giving the Callable and the lambda parameter explicit types, as above, avoids it. Java ignores the annotation.

worked.title: Unblock a ledger verticle, step by step

steps.say: A balance consumer calls JDBC directly. It works in a demo with one request. Under load, every handler on the same event loop waits behind it, and the blocked-thread checker stays silent: it measures one task at a time, and each 300 ms query is under its 2-second limit. Short blocking calls are the kind that never show up in the logs.
steps.code: vertx.eventBus().<String>consumer("ledger.balance", msg -> { try { msg.reply(LedgerDao.balanceCents(msg.body())); // 300 ms on the event loop } catch (InterruptedException e) { msg.fail(500, "interrupted"); } });

alt.html: vertx.eventBus().consumer<String>("ledger.balance") { msg -> msg.reply(LedgerDao.balanceCents(msg.body())) // 300 ms on the event loop }

steps.say: First attempt: executeBlocking with the default. The loop is free now, but six concurrent requests still take about 6 × 300 ms, because they all come from this consumer's context and the default is ordered.
steps.code: vertx.executeBlocking(() -> LedgerDao.balanceCents(msg.body())) // ordered: one at a time .onSuccess(msg::reply);

alt.html: vertx.executeBlocking(Callable<Long> { LedgerDao.balanceCents(msg.body()) }) // ordered: one at a time .onSuccess { cents: Long -> msg.reply(cents) }

steps.say: Second attempt: unordered. The queries now overlap on the worker pool, and the replies still come back on the consumer's context. The lab's test checks both: total time under 1,000 ms for six queries, and an event-loop lag under 150 ms.
steps.code: vertx.executeBlocking(() -> LedgerDao.balanceCents(msg.body()), false) // independent calls .onSuccess(msg::reply) .onFailure(e -> msg.fail(500, e.getMessage()));

alt.html: vertx.executeBlocking(Callable<Long> { LedgerDao.balanceCents(msg.body()) }, false) // independent calls .onSuccess { cents: Long -> msg.reply(cents) } .onFailure { e -> msg.fail(500, e.message) }

steps.say: Another design gives you a visible concurrency limit: make the whole verticle a worker and deploy as many instances as you want parallel queries. Each instance handles one message at a time on the worker pool, so four instances means at most four queries in flight, which you can match to the JDBC pool.
steps.code: vertx.deployVerticle(BlockingBalanceVerticle::new, new DeploymentOptions() .setThreadingModel(ThreadingModel.WORKER) // may block .setInstances(4)); // at most 4 queries at once

alt.html: vertx.deployVerticle(::BlockingBalanceVerticle, DeploymentOptions() .setThreadingModel(ThreadingModel.WORKER) // may block .setInstances(4)) // at most 4 queries at once

lab.title: Request/reply on the event bus, then unblock a verticle
steps: Run the tests. All five fail: AuthorizeVerticle.start() throws, so the deployment in @BeforeEach fails.

Write AuthorizeVerticle.start(): register a JsonObject consumer on ADDRESS, approve amounts up to LIMIT with a reply {status, card, thread}, fail larger ones with msg.fail(402, "limit exceeded"), and return the consumer's completion(). Four tests should pass.
Read balanceQueriesDoNotBlockTheLoop. It makes its own Vertx with one event loop, sends six requests, and measures both the event-loop lag and the total time.
Fix BalanceVerticle with executeBlocking. Try the one-argument version first and read the failure, then pass false.
hints: msg.body().getDouble("amount") reads the amount; Thread.currentThread().getName() gives the thread value.
msg.fail(402, "limit exceeded") reaches the requester as a ReplyException with failureType() RECIPIENT_FAILURE and failureCode() 402.

If a test times out after 30 seconds instead of failing fast, an assertion probably ran outside tc.verify(...). The test file writes @io.vertx.junit5.Timeout in full because JUnit's own @Timeout has the same simple name.
lab.done: All five tests in VerticleTest pass, and you have seen the ordered executeBlocking fail the total-time assertion.

drill.title: Write a verticle that offloads a blocking call
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write a VerticleBase that answers requests on ledger.balance by running the blocking LedgerDao.balanceCents(account) off the event loop, in parallel across requests, and fails the message with code 500 on error. Then write the line that deploys two instances.

answer.html: public class BalanceVerticle extends VerticleBase { @Override public Future<?> start() { return vertx.eventBus().<String>consumer("ledger.balance", msg -> vertx.executeBlocking(() -> LedgerDao.balanceCents(msg.body()), false) .onSuccess(msg::reply) // back on this verticle's context .onFailure(e -> msg.fail(500, e.getMessage())) ).completion(); } } vertx.deployVerticle(BalanceVerticle::new, new DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2));

alt.html: class BalanceVerticle : VerticleBase() { override fun start(): Future<*> = vertx.eventBus().consumer<String>("ledger.balance") { msg -> val query = Callable<Long> { LedgerDao.balanceCents(msg.body()) } vertx.executeBlocking(query, false) .onSuccess { cents: Long -> msg.reply(cents) } // back on this verticle's context .onFailure { e -> msg.fail(500, e.message) } }.completion() } vertx.deployVerticle(::BalanceVerticle, DeploymentOptions().setInstances(2))

recap: Vert.x runs on Netty event loops (2 × cores by default). A context ties code to one thread, and a handler never runs concurrently with itself.
Vert.x 5 is futures-only: async methods return Future, callback overloads are gone, and executeBlocking takes a Callable.
Each verticle instance gets its own context: EVENT_LOOP (never block), WORKER (may block, still one task at a time) or VIRTUAL_THREAD (Java 21+, await() parks).
The event bus offers send, request and publish on string addresses. Requests fail with NO_HANDLERS, RECIPIENT_FAILURE or TIMEOUT; the default timeout is 30 s, and delivery is best effort.
The blocked-thread checker warns after 2 s (checked every second) and adds a stack trace after 5 s. It only reports.
executeBlocking is ordered per context by default. Pass false for independent calls, or use worker verticles with several instances.

explain.prompt: A colleague wrapped four slow JDBC calls in executeBlocking and is surprised that a burst of four requests still takes four times as long as one. Explain what a Vert.x context is and why their change didn't help, and what to do instead.
explain.answer: A context is where Vert.x runs a piece of code: a handler registered on a context always runs there, one task at a time. All requests to one HTTP server share that server's context. executeBlocking moves the callable to the worker pool, which frees the event loop, but by default it is ordered per context: Vert.x queues calls from the same context and runs them one after another. So the four queries still ran in sequence, just on a worker thread instead of the event loop. If the calls are independent, pass false as the second argument so they run in parallel on the worker pool, or deploy a worker verticle with several instances to get an explicit concurrency limit. Either way, size the parallelism to the JDBC connection pool behind it.

deeper.html:
Testing Vert.x code has its own traps, and vertx-junit5 exists because of them. A Vert.x callback runs on an event loop, after your test method has returned. If an assertion fails there, JUnit never sees it. The extension fixes that with VertxTestContext: the test passes only when you call completeNow() (or flag all checkpoints), and fails when you call failNow(...) or when an assertion inside tc.verify(() -> ...) throws.

This track's research ran the same failing assertion both ways. Outside verify, the test ran into the timeout after about 2.6 seconds with "The test execution timed out. Make sure your asynchronous code includes calls to either VertxTestContext#completeNow(), VertxTestContext#failNow() or Checkpoint#flag()", and the real AssertionFailedError was only printed to the log. Inside verify, it failed in 0.059 seconds with the actual assertion message. So every assertion in a callback goes inside verify, or inside tc.succeeding(...) and tc.failing(...), which wrap it for you.

Other details from the vertx-junit5 docs: the default timeout is 30 seconds, overridden per test with @io.vertx.junit5.Timeout (fully qualified, to avoid JUnit's @Timeout). A Vertx injected into a @BeforeAll method is shared by the class, one injected into @BeforeEach is shared by that test and its @AfterEach, and injected instances are closed for you. tc.checkpoint(n) gives a counter that must be flagged n times, handy for testing publish to several consumers. And in Vert.x 5, clients rely on Cleaner, so a client object that becomes unreachable can close its pool while a test still uses it. Keep clients in fields during tests.
